docs.title: LynxPrompt
docs.text:
LynxPrompt is a self-hosted web app that turns one set of AI coding rules into the file each tool reads: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursor/rules/, Copilot instructions, 30 rule-file formats in all, plus slash commands for six of them. A wizard writes the rules from your stack, blueprints let a team share them with variables, and the CLI and the VS Code extension put the files into every repository.

This site is about running your own instance: start with Docker Compose, then the settings, the CLI and how it is built. The product manual (the wizard step by step, blueprints, the CLI and API reference) is a separate site at lynxprompt.geiser.cloud/docs, and lynxprompt.geiser.cloud is a hosted instance you can try without installing anything.

  • Run with Docker

    Three commands start the app and PostgreSQL, and the Mailpit link signs you in. A Helm chart covers Kubernetes.

  • Your first sign-in

    How the magic link works, how to read it without a mail server, and what the dashboard looks like when it worked.

  • The CLI and the VS Code extension

    lynxp wizard, pull, push and diff against your instance, and the same from inside VS Code.

  • Environment variables

    Every setting with its default, and the five you need for sign-in.

docs.title: The web app
docs.text:
The wizard asks about the project, the stack, the commands, the code style and the boundaries, then writes the files for the tools you pick. Usage walks through the wizard, the blueprint pages, the dashboard and teams.

The wizard

Blueprints

One blueprint

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Keeps one set of rules for 26 coding agents in one AGENTS.md, with an import, a config or a full copy for the tools that do not read it directly (the list is in Features), plus slash commands for 18 of them.
  • Builds those rules in a 12-step wizard on the web, or with lynxp wizard in a terminal; lynxp analyze reads an existing repository first.
  • Keeps blueprints with [[VARIABLE|default]] placeholders, so one blueprint fits many projects. Each blueprint is private, shared with a team, or public.
  • Gives a team its own page and its own blueprints. An opt-in federation lists the instances that join in a shared directory.
  • Manages hierarchical AGENTS.md files for monorepos, from the dashboard, the CLI (lynxp hierarchies) and the API.
  • Serves the same data to the CLI, the VS Code extension and a REST API with per-token roles.
  • Signs users in with a magic link, passkeys, GitHub or Google OAuth, or OIDC SSO; each is one environment variable.
  • Edits blueprints with Claude when you set your own Anthropic API key; off by default, and everything else works without it.

docs.title: How it runs
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    BR[Browser]
    CLI[lynxp CLI<br/>VS Code extension<br/>GitHub Action]
    subgraph app [lynxprompt container, port 3000]
        WEB[Next.js app and API]
        MIG[prisma migrate deploy on start]
    end
    DB[(PostgreSQL<br/>app, users, blog, support schemas)]
    SMTP[Your SMTP server<br/>sign-in mail]
    OPT[Optional: GitHub or Google OAuth,<br/>SSO provider, Anthropic API]
    FED[Other instances<br/>public blueprints]

    BR <--> WEB
    CLI <-->|API token| WEB
    WEB --> DB
    MIG --> DB
    WEB --> SMTP
    WEB -.-> OPT
    WEB <-.-> FED
  • The image is drumsergio/lynxprompt, built for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, running as user id 1001.
  • Migrations run every time the container starts (prisma migrate deploy on the four schemas), so an upgrade is a tag change and docker compose up -d.
  • The self-host compose file runs one PostgreSQL server with one database per schema (lynxprompt, lynxprompt_users, lynxprompt_blog, lynxprompt_support). See Components.
  • The CLI and the extension talk to /api/v1/ with an API token you create in Settings. See How it works.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• It does not send mail by itself. The default login is a magic link, so a real deployment needs the five SMTP_* variables; the Mailpit file is only for trying it out.
  • It does not run your AI tools. It writes the files they read.
  • It does not edit with AI unless you give it an Anthropic API key.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
• Accounts, blueprints, drafts and teams live in your PostgreSQL; avatars, team logos and blog images live in the uploads volume. Back up both volumes and you have everything.
  • Every other outside service is off until you switch it on with an environment variable: SMTP for sign-in mail, GitHub and Google for OAuth, an SSO provider, Anthropic for AI editing, Cloudflare Turnstile, Umami analytics. The exception is Gravatar: an account without a profile picture shows a Gravatar image, so browsers request gravatar.com with a hash of that account's email address. See Configuration.
  • Federation is off by default. With ENABLE_FEDERATION=true, at start and every six hours the instance sends its domain (the host of APP_URL) to the registry at lynxprompt.geiser.cloud, and /.well-known/lynxprompt.json answers with its name, version and number of public blueprints. /api/v1/federation/blueprints lists the name, description, tags and author of public blueprints; nothing private is listed, and no blueprint content is sent anywhere. Unless it is turned on, the instance makes no call to the registry.
  • The security policy is in SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text:
• If something is broken, read Troubleshooting, then open an issue with the details in Reporting a bug.
  • To report a security problem, follow the security policy and do not open a public issue.
  • The releases page lists what changed in each version.
  • To send a fix or a feature, read Development and CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Every setting is an environment variable read by the container. docker-compose.selfhost.yml takes them from .env; the Helm chart maps them from values.yaml. Defaults below are what the app uses when the variable is unset; "compose" means the self-host compose file sets it for you.

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Variable Default What it does NEXTAUTH_SECRET none, required Signs sessions. openssl rand -base64 32. Changing it signs everyone out. DB_PASSWORD none, required Used by the compose file for PostgreSQL and for the four DB_*_PASSWORD values below. APP_URL http://localhost:3000 The URL browsers use. Sign-in links and OAuth callbacks are built from it; the compose file also sets NEXTAUTH_URL to it. ADMIN_EMAIL empty Compose only: copied into SUPERADMIN_EMAIL. When it is empty, SUPERADMIN_EMAIL from .env is used. SUPERADMIN_EMAIL empty The account with this address becomes superadmin when it signs in. PORT 3000 Compose only: the host port published for the app.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
The entrypoint builds one connection string per schema (app, users, blog, support) from these, unless the full DATABASE_URL_APP, DATABASE_URL_USERS, DATABASE_URL_BLOG or DATABASE_URL_SUPPORT is set. The self-host compose file uses one PostgreSQL server and one database per schema: lynxprompt, lynxprompt_users, lynxprompt_blog and lynxprompt_support. The first start creates lynxprompt_users. The blog and support databases are only created and migrated while ENABLE_BLOG or ENABLE_SUPPORT_FORUM is on, so an instance without those features runs on two databases. Turning a feature off leaves its database as it is, and turning it back on migrates it from where it stopped. Never point two schemas at the same database: prisma db push drops the tables it does not know, so each start would delete the other schema's tables.

Variable (per APP, USERS, BLOG, SUPPORT) Default What it does DB_<NAME>_HOST compose: postgres PostgreSQL host DB_<NAME>_PORT 5432 Port DB_<NAME>_USER compose: lynxprompt User DB_<NAME>_PASSWORD compose: DB_PASSWORD Password DB_<NAME>_NAME compose: lynxprompt, lynxprompt_users, lynxprompt_blog, lynxprompt_support Database name, one per schema DB_<NAME>_SCHEMA public Schema DATABASE_URL_<NAME> built from the above Full connection string; wins when set Variable Default What it does DB_SSL false true makes the app's own connections to PostgreSQL use TLS. The migrations at start connect with the connection string as written. DB_SSL_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED true With DB_SSL=true, false accepts a server certificate that does not verify, such as a self-signed one.

docs.title: Sign-in
docs.text: Variable Default What it does ENABLE_EMAIL_AUTH true Magic-link login by mail. Needs the SMTP_* variables. SMTP_HOST empty Mail server for the sign-in link. Without it, no one can sign in by mail. SMTP_PORT 587 465 switches to implicit TLS. SMTP_USER, SMTP_PASSWORD empty Mail server login. The app logs in whenever the server offers AUTH, so a server that offers it needs both. SMTP_FROM noreply@<host of APP_URL> Sender address. ENABLE_PASSKEYS true WebAuthn passkeys, for accounts that already exist. ENABLE_GITHUB_OAUTH false GitHub login. Needs GITHUB_CLIENT_ID and GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET; callback <APP_URL>/api/auth/callback/github. ENABLE_GOOGLE_OAUTH false Google login. Needs GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET; callback <APP_URL>/api/auth/callback/google. ENABLE_SSO false OpenID Connect sign-in, configured per team in the UI. A team's IdP signs in only addresses on a domain the team verified with a TXT record at _lynxprompt-sso.<domain>. Needs SSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY. SSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY empty 64 hex characters (32 bytes, openssl rand -hex 32). Encrypts the SSO client secrets at rest; without it a team cannot save an SSO configuration. Keep it: changing it makes the stored secrets unreadable. SSO_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IDP false true lets a team's IdP live on a private or loopback address and use plain http://. Leave it off on an instance strangers can sign up to: the server calls the IdP's URLs itself. ENABLE_USER_REGISTRATION true false lets only existing accounts and addresses with a pending team invitation sign in (others get RegistrationDisabled). ENABLE_TURNSTILE false Cloudflare Turnstile on the sign-in forms. Needs both keys below. NEXT_PUBLIC_TURNSTILE_SITE_KEY empty Turnstile site key, read when the container starts. TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY empty Turnstile secret key. With ENABLE_TURNSTILE=true and no secret, the server skips the check.

docs.title: Client address
docs.text:
Rate limits and download counts key on the client's address, so the app needs to know which header your proxy writes.

Variable Default What it does TRUSTED_PROXY 1 How many reverse proxies sit in front of the app. The app reads the X-Forwarded-For entry that many places from the right, the one your outermost proxy wrote; anything to its left came from the client. cloudflare reads CF-Connecting-IP instead; set it only when the app cannot be reached except through Cloudflare. With no proxy at all, a client can choose its own X-Forwarded-For, so put the app behind one.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
Variable Default What it does APP_NAME LynxPrompt Name shown in the UI and in mail. APP_LOGO_URL empty Your own logo in the sign-in mail and in search-engine metadata. The header keeps the LynxPrompt logo. ENABLE_AI false AI editing of blueprints. Needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. AI_MODEL claude-haiku-5-5 Model used for AI editing. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY empty Your Anthropic key; only read when ENABLE_AI=true. ENABLE_BLOG false The blog module. Its database is migrated only while this is on. ENABLE_SUPPORT_FORUM false The support forum module. Its database is migrated only while this is on. UMAMI_SCRIPT_URL empty Umami analytics script. Loaded only when NEXT_PUBLIC_UMAMI_WEBSITE_ID is set too. NEXT_PUBLIC_UMAMI_WEBSITE_ID empty Umami website id. CONTACT_EMAIL info@<host of APP_URL> Where the contact form sends. The form needs SMTP_HOST, SMTP_USER and SMTP_PASSWORD, so it does not work against a mail server without a login. STATUS_PAGE_URL empty Status page link in the footer. UPLOAD_DIR /data/uploads/blog Where blog images go; avatars and team logos go one level up. The self-host compose file mounts the uploads volume at /data/uploads. ENABLE_FEDERATION false true registers the instance's domain with the federation registry at start and every six hours, and serves /.well-known/lynxprompt.json. Needs an APP_URL on https with a public domain name. Off, the instance makes no call to the registry. FEDERATION_REGISTRY_URL https://lynxprompt.geiser.cloud The registry the instance registers with.

The CLI has two settings of its own: lynxp config set-url <url> (stored in the file lynxp config path prints) and the LYNXPROMPT_API_URL environment variable, which wins when set. See Usage.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Frontend + API: Next.js 16 with App Router
  • Database: PostgreSQL with Prisma ORM
  • Deployment: Docker Compose with auto-migration on startup
  • Auth: NextAuth.js with configurable providers
  • Search: Full-text search via PostgreSQL

Four Prisma schemas (app, users, blog, support), each in its own database. One PostgreSQL server can hold all four; two schemas must never share a database, because prisma db push drops the tables it does not know.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/GeiserX/LynxPrompt.git
cd LynxPrompt
docker run -d --name lynxprompt-db -p 5432:5432 -e POSTGRES_USER=lynxprompt -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=changeme postgres:18-alpine
for db in app users blog support; do docker exec lynxprompt-db createdb -U lynxprompt lynxprompt_$db; done
cp env.example .env   # uncomment the four DATABASE_URL_* lines (Option A)
npm install
set -a; . ./.env; set +a   # Prisma 7 does not read .env by itself
npm run db:generate
npm run db:push
npm run dev

A schema change needs a migration, because the image applies migrations, not the schema. Write it from the difference to the schema on main, which needs no database (here for the users schema):

git show origin/main:prisma/schema-users.prisma > /tmp/old.prisma
dir=prisma/migrations-users/$(date -u +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)_add_something
mkdir -p "$dir"
npx prisma migrate diff --config=prisma/prisma.config-users.ts \
  --from-schema /tmp/old.prisma --to-schema prisma/schema-users.prisma --script -o "$dir/migration.sql"

docker compose up -d with the root docker-compose.yml starts the full stack, app included, on port 3000; its databases publish no port, so npm run dev cannot reach them. Use it to run the image, not to develop.

See CONTRIBUTING.md for contribution guidelines.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
The site is MkDocs Material, built strictly:

pip install -r docs/requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs build --strict     # any broken link or unreachable page fails it
mkdocs serve

docs.yml builds every pull request and deploys main into the gh-pages branch next to the Helm repository's index.yaml, which it never touches.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
LynxPrompt is a self-hostable platform for managing AI IDE configuration files, AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules/, CLAUDE.md and 30 rule-file formats in all, plus slash commands for six of them. Deploy it on your own infrastructure and give your team a central hub to create, share, and standardize AI coding assistant configurations across every project.

Instead of manually writing configuration files for every project and every AI tool, use LynxPrompt to:

  • Generate configs through an interactive wizard (web or CLI)
  • Share blueprints with your team, or publicly, through your instance's marketplace
  • Standardize AI behavior across projects with reusable templates
  • Export to any supported format with one click

LynxPrompt is free and open-source. Self-host it for personal use, or deploy it within your organization to enforce coding standards, share institutional knowledge, and ensure consistent AI assistant behavior across your engineering teams. A hosted instance is also available at lynxprompt.geiser.cloud for those who prefer not to self-host.

docs.title: Universal AI Config Hub
docs.text: Rules for 26 coding agents: Codex, Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Devin Desktop (formerly Windsurf), Antigravity, Zed, Aider, Gemini CLI, Cline, Zoo Code, Junie, Kiro, Goose, Warp, Grok Build, Pi and more. Write the rules once: pick several tools and LynxPrompt keeps them in one AGENTS.md, which most of these agents read directly. Claude Code and Gemini CLI get a CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md that imports it, Aider a .aider.conf.yml that loads it, and the tools that cannot reach it (Copilot, Trae, Tabnine) a full copy. Slash commands for Cursor, Claude Code, Devin Desktop, Copilot, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Kiro, Junie, Augment, Trae, Kilo Code, Cline, Zoo Code, Crush, Firebender, Factory, Qwen Code and Pi. MCP server configs are blueprints too: one config downloads or converts to the MCP file of 24 tools (.mcp.json, .cursor/mcp.json, .vscode/mcp.json, .gemini/settings.json, .zed/settings.json, opencode.json, .codex/config.toml and more), and the CLI writes into a settings file without touching its other settings. The CLI wizard can list your MCP servers in the generated rules; it does not write MCP configuration files.

docs.title: Blueprint Marketplace
docs.text: Internal marketplace for sharing AI configurations and slash commands within your organization. Browse, search, favorite, and reuse blueprints across teams. Search and downloads cover the blueprints of your own instance; the opt-in federation lists instances in a shared directory but does not bring other instances' blueprints into your marketplace.

docs.title: Interactive Wizard
docs.text: Step-by-step config generator available on both web and CLI. Auto-detects your tech stack, frameworks, and repo structure from GitHub/GitLab URLs. Supports template variables, monorepo hierarchies, and draft auto-saving.

docs.title: Agent Skills and Subagents
docs.text: Store an Agent Skill (SKILL.md) or a subagent once and write it where every agent reads it. A skill goes to .agents/skills/<name>/ (Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Zed, Junie and most others) and .claude/skills/<name>/ (Claude Code), plus Kiro and Firebender when picked. A subagent goes to .claude/agents/ and .agents/agents/, plus .github/agents/<name>.agent.md for Copilot and .codex/agents/<name>.toml for Codex when picked. The web download and lynxp pull write the same copies, and lynxp push keeps them in step.

docs.title: Configurable Authentication
docs.text:
Flexible auth to fit your environment:

  • OAuth — GitHub, Google
  • Email — Passwordless magic link login
  • Passkeys — WebAuthn biometric/hardware key authentication
  • SSO — OpenID Connect for enterprise identity providers

docs.title: Optional AI-Powered Editing
docs.text: Enable AI-assisted blueprint creation and editing with your own Anthropic API key. Entirely optional — works fully without it.

docs.title: Full REST API + CLI Tool
docs.text: Programmatic access for automation and CI/CD integration. Generate API tokens, fetch blueprints, search, and download via REST. The CLI (lynxp) mirrors the full web platform feature set.

docs.title: Self-Hostable with Docker Compose
docs.text:
Single docker compose up to run the entire stack. PostgreSQL included. Auto-runs database migrations on startup. Toggle every feature via environment variables.

The product manual at lynxprompt.geiser.cloud/docs describes each feature from the user's side.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: LynxPrompt runs as one container next to PostgreSQL. You need Docker with Compose v2 (or Kubernetes for the Helm chart) and, for a real deployment, an SMTP server: the default way to sign in is a link sent by mail. The image is built for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, so Apple Silicon, Raspberry Pi and other ARM hosts run it natively.

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GeiserX/LynxPrompt/main/docker-compose.selfhost.yml -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GeiserX/LynxPrompt/main/docker-compose.mailpit.yml
(umask 077; printf 'NEXTAUTH_SECRET=%s\nDB_PASSWORD=%s\nADMIN_EMAIL=you@example.com\n' "$(openssl rand -base64 32)" "$(openssl rand -hex 24)" > .env)
docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml -f docker-compose.mailpit.yml up -d

What the three lines do:

  1. Download the compose file and, for a try-out, the Mailpit file. Mailpit is a local mailbox that catches the sign-in mail so you can read the link at http://localhost:8025 without an SMTP server.
  2. Write a .env only you can read: the session secret, the database password and your own address in ADMIN_EMAIL. That address becomes the superadmin the first time it signs in.
  3. Start PostgreSQL and the app. The first start pulls the image and runs the migrations; docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml -f docker-compose.mailpit.yml logs -f lynxprompt shows Database sync complete. and then the Next.js ready line.

The app listens on http://localhost:3000. PORT=8080 in .env moves it, and APP_URL must then be the URL the browser uses (http://localhost:8080, or your domain behind a reverse proxy), because the sign-in link is built from it.

docs.title: First sign-in
docs.text:
Open http://localhost:3000/auth/signin and enter the ADMIN_EMAIL address. LynxPrompt mails a link that is valid for 24 hours. With the Mailpit file, open http://localhost:8025 and click the link there; the dashboard opens, with Quick Actions, your blueprints, drafts and teams. That account is promoted to superadmin at that sign-in (the promotion happens whenever the signed-in address equals SUPERADMIN_EMAIL, which the compose file sets from ADMIN_EMAIL).

For a real deployment, put your mail server in .env and leave the Mailpit file out of the docker compose line:

SMTP_HOST=smtp.example.com
SMTP_PORT=587
SMTP_USER=lynxprompt
SMTP_PASSWORD=...
SMTP_FROM=lynxprompt@example.com

Never expose Mailpit: anyone who can open its port can sign in as anyone. The other ways to sign in (passkeys, GitHub or Google OAuth, SSO) are switched on in Configuration; passkeys need an account that already exists, so the first sign-in is always the mail link or OAuth.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: Change the image tag in docker-compose.selfhost.yml to the newer release from Docker Hub and run the same docker compose ... up -d. Migrations run at start. Back up the four databases first (docker compose ... exec postgres pg_dumpall -U lynxprompt > backup.sql). Uploaded images live in the uploads volume, which survives the upgrade.

docs.title: Helm chart (Kubernetes)
docs.text:
helm repo add lynxprompt https://geiserx.github.io/LynxPrompt
helm install lynxprompt lynxprompt/lynxprompt

The chart bundles PostgreSQL by default, or points at an external one with externalDatabase.*. Its values are documented in the chart README and listed in values.yaml. The chart is also on ArtifactHub.

docs.title: Install channels
docs.text:
What Channel Command or link Web app Docker Hub drumsergio/lynxprompt (tags) Web app Helm helm repo add lynxprompt https://geiserx.github.io/LynxPrompt Web app Hosted instance lynxprompt.geiser.cloud, no install CLI lynxp npm npm install -g lynxprompt CLI lynxp Homebrew (macOS, Linux) brew install GeiserX/lynxprompt/lynxprompt CLI lynxp Chocolatey (Windows) choco install lynxprompt CLI lynxp AUR (Arch) lynxprompt (still 2.1.1 for now; npm and Homebrew carry the current version) CLI lynxp Snap snap install lynxprompt CLI lynxp Binaries attached to each release VS Code Marketplace LynxPrompt.lynxprompt, or ext install LynxPrompt.lynxprompt CI GitHub Action lynxprompt-action AI assistants MCP server lynxprompt-mcp

After installing the CLI: lynxp config set-url https://lynxprompt.example.com for your own instance (the default, which lynxp config show prints, is the hosted instance at https://lynxprompt.geiser.cloud), then lynxp login. See Usage.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• The app: one Next.js 16 process (App Router) that serves the pages and the API on port 3000, running as user id 1001 in the drumsergio/lynxprompt image (linux/amd64).
  • PostgreSQL with four Prisma schemas: app (platforms, languages, frameworks, wizard steps, system templates, federated instances), users (accounts, sessions, passkeys, teams, blueprints, drafts, hierarchies, API tokens), blog and support (the two optional modules). Each schema has its own database, because prisma db push drops the tables it does not know; the self-host compose file keeps the four databases on one PostgreSQL server.
  • Migrations run at every start: the entrypoint builds the four connection strings from the DB_* variables, runs prisma migrate deploy for each schema, and refuses to start if one fails. A database that an earlier release built with prisma db push gets one last db push of the schema as the first migration (0_init) created it, which refuses any change that would lose data. Only 0_init is then recorded as applied, so every later migration runs as written.
  • Mail: the sign-in link is sent through your SMTP server with nodemailer. Nothing else is mailed unless the contact form is on.
flowchart LR
    BR[Browser] <--> WEB[Next.js pages and API]
    CLI[lynxp CLI, VS Code extension,<br/>GitHub Action, MCP server] <-->|Bearer API token| WEB
    WEB --> DB[(PostgreSQL: app, users,<br/>blog, support)]
    WEB --> SMTP[SMTP server]
    WEB -.-> EXT[GitHub or Google OAuth, SSO,<br/>Anthropic API: optional]
    WEB <-.->|public blueprints| FED[Other LynxPrompt instances]

docs.title: Sign-in
docs.text: NextAuth with database sessions (30 days, refreshed daily). The providers are built from the feature flags: the mail link (ENABLE_EMAIL_AUTH, on by default, needs SMTP_*), passkeys (ENABLE_PASSKEYS, for existing accounts), GitHub and Google OAuth, and OIDC SSO per team, limited to the email domains the team verified in DNS. When an account whose address equals SUPERADMIN_EMAIL signs in by any method but SSO, it is promoted to superadmin. Roles are USER, ADMIN and SUPERADMIN. With ENABLE_USER_REGISTRATION=false, an address without an account is refused with RegistrationDisabled, unless it has a pending, unexpired team invitation.

docs.title: What the CLI and the extension talk to
docs.text: lynxp login opens the configured instance in the browser (lynxp config set-url, or LYNXPROMPT_API_URL) and stores an API token in a file only its owner can read. The CLI keeps one token per instance, so switching with lynxp config set-url keeps the other logins and asks the new instance whether its saved token still works. A token is sent only to the instance that issued it, and lynxp logout revokes the current instance's token there. Every call after that is Authorization: Bearer <token> against /api/v1/. Tokens are created in Settings, carry a role (BLUEPRINTS_FULL, BLUEPRINTS_READONLY, PROFILE_FULL and others) and an expiry, and the API answers 401 with the settings URL when one expires. The VS Code extension, the GitHub Action and the MCP server use the same API with the same tokens.

docs.title: Blueprints, variables and hierarchies
docs.text: A blueprint is text plus a name, a description, a type, a category, tags and a visibility (private, team, public). [[VARIABLE|default]] placeholders are filled at download time. A hierarchy links several AGENTS.md blueprints to paths of one repository, for monorepos; the API exposes it at /api/v1/hierarchies and the CLI as lynxp hierarchies.

docs.title: Federation
docs.text: Federation is off by default, and an instance makes no call to the registry until ENABLE_FEDERATION=true. Then, at start and every six hours after, it posts its domain (the host of APP_URL) to the registry (FEDERATION_REGISTRY_URL, lynxprompt.geiser.cloud by default) and serves /.well-known/lynxprompt.json with its name, version, API URL and number of public blueprints. An APP_URL that is not https on a public domain name (such as http://localhost:3000) is skipped with a warning, since the registry could not reach it. The registry lists the instances on /federation, and each instance lists the name, description, tags and author of its public blueprints at /api/v1/federation/blueprints; no instance pulls another's blueprints into its own marketplace. Private and team blueprints never leave the instance. These public reads carry a five-minute public Cache-Control, so a CDN in front of the instance can serve them.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
• Secrets come from environment variables; nothing is read from files in the image.
  • Sessions use secure, HttpOnly cookies with the __Secure- prefix in production.
  • The app rate-limits by client address in memory, per instance: 5000 requests per minute in general and 300 per minute on the sign-in endpoints, answering 429 with Retry-After.
  • Every response carries X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, a Referrer-Policy, a Permissions-Policy, a Content-Security-Policy and, in production, HSTS.
  • The container runs as a non-root user; the compose file publishes only the app port, never PostgreSQL.
  • Reporting: SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Where the data is
docs.text: Everything is in PostgreSQL, in the pgdata volume of the compose file. A backup is pg_dumpall of that server; a restore is psql into an empty one before the first start. Uploaded files (blog and profile images) live in the app container's uploads path; the Helm chart gives them a volume.

docs.title: The sign-in mail never arrives
docs.text: The default login sends a link by mail through SMTP_HOST, and the self-host compose file sets no mail server. docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml logs lynxprompt shows a nodemailer connection error after each attempt. Fix: set SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT, SMTP_USER, SMTP_PASSWORD and SMTP_FROM in .env and restart, or add -f docker-compose.mailpit.yml to try it out and read the link at http://localhost:8025. See First sign-in.

docs.title: The link in the mail points at localhost, or at the wrong port
docs.text: The link is built from APP_URL. Set it to the URL the browser uses (https://lynxprompt.example.com, or http://localhost:8080 when PORT=8080) and restart.

docs.title: "Registration is disabled" on sign-in
docs.text: ENABLE_USER_REGISTRATION=false and the address has no account yet. Invite the address to a team first: a pending, unexpired team invitation lets that address create its account and accept. Or create the account with registration on.

docs.title: My account is not the superadmin
docs.text: The promotion happens at sign-in when the address equals SUPERADMIN_EMAIL, ignoring case (the compose file copies ADMIN_EMAIL into it). Check the value with docker compose ... exec lynxprompt printenv SUPERADMIN_EMAIL, fix .env, restart and sign in again.

docs.title: The container fails to start with a database error
docs.text: The entrypoint runs prisma migrate deploy on four schemas and exits if one fails. The log names the schema. Usual causes: PostgreSQL not ready yet (the compose file waits for its healthcheck, a hand-written one may not), a wrong DB_*_PASSWORD, or a PostgreSQL 18 volume mounted at /var/lib/postgresql/data instead of /var/lib/postgresql (the compose file has the right path and a comment).

docs.title: Start fails with "DB predates 0_init and holds data of features since removed"
docs.text: The database comes from a release older than 2.0.43 that still holds rows of a feature LynxPrompt has since removed, such as the seller payouts and blueprint prices. The entrypoint brings an old database to the first migration with one prisma db push, which refuses to drop data, and lists above that line what it would drop. The database it names is left as it was, though another one may already have been upgraded in the same start, so go back to the earlier image only with the backup. To upgrade, back up the databases, then start once with BASELINE_ACCEPT_DATA_LOSS=true in .env (on Kubernetes, in the chart's extraEnv); the listed data is deleted and every later migration runs. Remove the variable afterwards. Old blueprint tiers are kept without it: SIMPLE becomes SHORT and ADVANCED becomes LONG.

docs.title: Sign-in fails with "The table public.User does not exist"
docs.text: Two schemas point at the same database. prisma db push drops the tables it does not know, so each push at start deletes the tables of the one before, and only the last schema's tables survive. Self-host compose files fetched before this page was written had that layout. Take the current docker-compose.selfhost.yml, which gives each schema its own database, and start again; if you set DB_*_NAME or DATABASE_URL_* yourself, give each of the four its own database.

docs.title: Pull or start fails on an ARM host
docs.text: The image is built for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, and Docker pulls the one that matches the host. If it fails with exec format error, an override forces the other architecture: remove any platform: line you added to the compose file, or DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM from the environment, and pull again.

docs.title: Port 3000 is already in use
docs.text: Set PORT=<free port> and APP_URL=http://localhost:<free port> in .env.

docs.title: lynxp talks to lynxprompt.geiser.cloud instead of my instance
docs.text:
The CLI defaults to the hosted instance, https://lynxprompt.geiser.cloud (lynxp config show prints the current value). Run lynxp config set-url https://lynxprompt.example.com, or set LYNXPROMPT_API_URL, which wins over the config file, then lynxp login again.

The hosted instance moved from https://lynxprompt.com. A CLI from 3.1.0 or older keeps that address in its config file; a newer CLI rewrites it, and the login saved for it, to the new one on its next run.

docs.title: Reporting a bug
docs.text: Open an issue at https://github.com/GeiserX/LynxPrompt/issues with: the image tag (docker compose ... images), the host (OS, architecture, Docker version), the names of the ENABLE_* variables you set (never their values or any secret), and the last 50 lines of docker compose ... logs lynxprompt. For a security problem follow SECURITY.md instead.

docs.title: The web app
docs.text:
• Wizard (/wizard): twelve steps (Project Basics, Tech Stack, Repository Setup, Security, Commands, Code Style, AI Behavior, Boundaries, Testing Strategy, Static Files, Anything Else?, Generate). Every step is available to every account. It works signed out; sign in to keep the result as a blueprint or a draft.
  • Blueprints (/blueprints): the public list, searchable and sortable; each blueprint page shows the content, its [[VARIABLE|default]] placeholders, tags, the author and a download button. Your own blueprints are private, shared with a team or public.
  • Dashboard (/dashboard): Quick Actions, My Blueprints, Team Blueprints, Saved Drafts and the hierarchical AGENTS.md sets for monorepos.
  • Teams (/teams): create a team with a name and a slug, invite members (the invite is mailed when SMTP_* is set, and the team page always has a link to copy), and share blueprints with the team only. Team blueprints show on the dashboard.
  • Settings (/settings): profile, security (passkeys), API tokens.

docs.title: The CLI
docs.text:
The CLI tool mirrors the web platform and works against any LynxPrompt instance. By default it connects to lynxprompt.geiser.cloud, but you can point it to any self-hosted deployment.

# Install
npm install -g lynxprompt

# (Optional) Point to a self-hosted instance — two ways:
lynxp config set-url https://lynxprompt.your-company.com
# or: export LYNXPROMPT_API_URL=https://lynxprompt.your-company.com

# Authenticate (opens browser on the configured instance)
lynxp login

# Generate AI config files interactively
lynxp wizard

# Pull a blueprint
lynxp pull bp_abc123

# Push local configs
lynxp push

# View current CLI configuration
lynxp config

The API URL is stored in the CLI config file (see lynxp config path). The LYNXPROMPT_API_URL environment variable takes precedence if set.

Also available via Homebrew (brew install GeiserX/lynxprompt/lynxprompt) and Chocolatey (choco install lynxprompt).

A recording of lynxp wizard, check, push, diff and analyze against the hosted instance: demo.gif (6.5 MB). The full command reference is in the product manual.

docs.title: VS Code extension
docs.text:
Prefer managing configs without leaving the editor? LynxPrompt also has an official VS Code extension. The extension is LynxPrompt.lynxprompt on the Marketplace; source in lynxprompt-vscode.

From inside VS Code you can:

  • Browse your cloud blueprints and local AI config files in a dedicated sidebar
  • Pull AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursor/rules/, and more into the correct workspace paths
  • Diff local files against their cloud versions with the built-in editor
  • Push updates back to LynxPrompt without leaving VS Code

Install it from the Marketplace or run ext install LynxPrompt.lynxprompt.

docs.title: The API
docs.text: Create a token in Settings > API Tokens (/settings?tab=api-tokens); tokens have a role (full or read-only blueprint access, profile access) and an expiry. Send it as Authorization: Bearer <token> to /api/v1/: GET and POST /api/v1/blueprints, /api/v1/hierarchies, /api/v1/user. The API reference in the product manual lists every field.
